verses.translation_literal: YHWH has become king; majesty he has put on; he has put on, YHWH, strength, he has girded himself; also, it is established, [the] world, not it will be shaken.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is king. He has put on majesty like a robe; the LORD has put on strength and cinched it at the waist. And so the world stands fixed on its foundations, and it will not be shaken.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is an enthronement shout, the kind a crowd gives when a new king takes his seat: "YHWH malak!" Say it as an announcement, not a report. The verb is a perfect, so the sense is "has become king" or "has taken up the kingship"; the KJV's present "reigneth" is smooth but loses the moment of acclamation. Rashi and Radak read it as a cry the nations will raise at the end of days. The Targum, for what it is worth, also has a perfect (meliKh), so it does not soften the verb into a future.

The clothing is the point. A king in the ancient Near East was known by his robes and his belt, and the psalm dresses God in two garments, ge'ut (majesty, from a root meaning to rise up) and 'oz (strength). The Hebrew gives three completed acts in a row: he put on majesty, he put on strength, he girded himself. The KJV keeps both "clothed" but turns the perfects into states ("is clothed"), and it folds the third act into a relative clause ("wherewith he hath girded himself"), so a sequence of deeds becomes a description with a footnote. The doubling of labesh, labesh is the drumbeat of the verse, and hit'azzar, "he girded himself", is the belt a warrior or workman tied before action. Ge'ut is usually human pride in the Bible; here only God wears it without sin. Ibn Ezra reads the clothing as a comparison from royal dress. The last colon says what kingship does: the world, tevel (the inhabited, fertile earth), is made firm. In a world where the chaos waters can undo it, a king's throne is cosmic insurance.

philological_notes.note: A perfect verb in an enthronement formula: 'YHWH has become king'. Compare the cry 'Absalom has become king' (2 Sam 15:10). Rashi and Radak take the whole as an acclamation of the future.
Reflexive: 'he girded himself'. The noun אֵזוֹר is a belt; Metzudat Zion glosses it as a girdle. Girding up the loins is what one does to act, to fight or to run.
The habitable, productive world, as distinct from אֶרֶץ 'earth, land'. It is the stage of human life that God's kingship keeps from toppling.

verses.translation_literal: Established [is] your throne from then; from long ago [are] you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your throne was set firm before any of this began. And you, you were there before the first day, from the age before ages.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera pulls back from the coronation to the long view. The king has just been acclaimed, yet the psalm insists the throne is not new: it was fixed "from then" (me'az), and God himself, now addressed as "you", is "from olam". Play the second half as a quiet, almost stunned address, because the psalm turns suddenly from "he" to "you".

The KJV's "of old" and "from everlasting" are fair, but "everlasting" suggests a philosophical eternity, while 'olam is the far, hidden horizon of time, the deep past that no one can see to the end of. Here is a likely contrast with neighbouring religions: in the Ugaritic texts Baal's kingship is won in battle against Yam, the Sea, and some scholars think it was re-enacted yearly, though that is one reading of the evidence. Here the throne is not a prize; it never lacked an owner. The Hebrew has no verb "art": the pronoun 'attah closes the verse like a seal, and the KJV's "thou art" is the natural English way to carry it. Radak and Metzudat David read the verse as 'since, and before, the creation of the world', Ibn Ezra as 'you have always sat on it'.

philological_notes.note: Nifal participle: 'established, set firm'. It is the same root as the verb of verse 1 (תִּכּוֹן), so the world's stability and the throne's stability are one thing.
'From the far past', the hidden time beyond reach, rather than abstract eternity. Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'before the world was created'.

verses.translation_literal: Rivers have lifted up, O YHWH, rivers have lifted up their voice; rivers lift up their pounding.
verses.translation_dramatic: The rivers have lifted up, LORD. The rivers have lifted up their voice, and now the rivers raise their roar, wave on wave, crashing, crashing.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here comes the threat, and it comes as sound. The word "rivers" arrives three times in one verse, each one louder than the last; the verse is a crescendo, so let your voice climb. The Hebrew nahar can be a river, but in this setting (a seam of the Canaanite myth of Yam, Sea, and Nahar, River, the enemies of the storm god) the "rivers" are the surging chaos waters that threaten to cancel the king's order. That myth is the background, and the psalm is polemic: the waters can roar, but they are only witnesses.

The KJV ("lifted up") keeps the verb, but "the floods" softens nehar into a weather event, and "waves" for the last word guesses at a hapax. The word dokhyam appears only here; Rashi ties it to a root meaning 'deep, low', Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra take it as breakers, and Radak links it to 'crush'. I have chosen 'pounding', because the root of 'crush' suits waves pounding on the shore. Notice also that the verb shifts from the perfect ("have lifted") to the imperfect ("lift"): the roar has begun and has not stopped. Rashi and Radak read the rivers as the nations; Ibn Ezra, as the sea and rivers always on the move.

philological_notes.note: 'Rivers', but in this psalm's mythic register the primeval waters, the same enemy as Sea (Yam) in verse 4. Radak reads the rivers as nations gathered for war.
A word found only here. Rashi derives it from דכא (low, deep); Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra take it as 'breakers'; Radak compares 'crush'. I follow the sense of pounding or crushing.

verses.translation_literal: More than the sounds of many waters, mighty [ones], breakers of [the] sea, mighty on high [is] YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Louder than the thunder of the great waters, mightier than the breakers of the sea, the LORD on high is mightier still.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse delays its subject until the very last word, so hold the breath: water, water, water, and then, only at the end, "YHWH". Everything before it is a comparison that the speaker piles up on purpose, so that the name lands like a door closing on the noise. The Hebrew reads: "More than the voices of many waters, the mighty ones, the breakers of the sea, mighty on high is YHWH."

The KJV rearranges this into "The Lord on high is mightier than the noise of many waters", which is sound English but moves the name to the front and so drains the surprise. It also turns 'adirim, a word used of the waters ('mighty ones'), into an adjective of the sea. The ASV keeps the Hebrew order better. A listener in Judah who had never seen the sea would know it from the Mediterranean, the western edge of the world, and from the Nile and Euphrates floods: forces no wall could hold. Malbim and Meiri see in the waters' limits the 'sand as a boundary' of Jeremiah 5:22, which is an echo of the same theme.

philological_notes.note: 'Mighty, majestic'. The word appears twice in the verse, once for the waters and once for YHWH, so the repetition is the argument: even the mightiest water is outmatched. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'strong'.
'Breakers', literally 'things that break', so waves breaking against the shore. Metzudat Zion says it means the waves of the sea.

verses.translation_literal: Your testimonies are very reliable; to your house befits holiness, O YHWH, for length of days.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your decrees stand firm, utterly sure. And holiness befits your house, beautiful and right, LORD, for as long as days go on.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes by stepping from the cosmos into the temple. After the thundering water, the voice drops: this is the congregation speaking to God in his own house. "Testimonies" ('edot) are what God has solemnly attested: his commands and promises, the covenant words. The Hebrew adds an intensifier, me'od, 'exceedingly', which the KJV's 'very sure' carries well.

The verse's real surprise is the last colon. The KJV and ASV end with "for ever", but the Hebrew has le'orekh yamim, 'for length of days', a phrase used of a long life or a lasting lease (compare Ps 23:6). It is not metaphysical eternity but 'for as long as there are days'. Radak and Metzudat David take it as a promise that the house will never again be destroyed. Rashi reads differently: the testimonies the prophets gave about the house stay faithful, however long the days are drawn out. The verb na'avah is related to na'veh, 'a dwelling'; Rashi notes it can be read as a word of dwelling, and Radak notes the unusual vowel under the aleph. 'Befits' covers both senses: holiness is what suits and adorns the house.

philological_notes.note: 'Your testimonies': what God has attested, his solemn commands and promises. Rashi reads it as what the prophets testified about the house.
'It is befitting, it is beautiful'. The vocalisation with the aleph is unusual, as Rashi and Radak both observe; Rashi links it to the sense of dwelling, Metzudat Zion to beauty.
'For length of days', not 'for ever'; it is the idiom of a long, lasting time.
